title: Chapter 17 — The Luxury Customer and How Luxury Selling Differs
intro: Who buys luxury appliances, what they are actually buying, and the posture the tier demands.

sections.title: Luxury Is a Different Sale
sections.content:
The luxury customer is not buying a refrigerator. They are buying a kitchen experience. They care about design, craftsmanship, brand heritage, and service — often more than they care about features or price.

The selling posture changes accordingly. Less pitching, more consulting. Less urgency, more patience. Less feature-dumping, more listening. The luxury customer expects to be understood, not sold to.

sections.title: The Consultation Model
sections.content:
Luxury sales often span multiple visits, involve designers and architects, and require project coordination over months. This is not a walk-in-and-close sale.

Treat it like a project. Build a relationship with the entire team — the homeowner, the designer, the contractor. Coordinate specifications, lead times, and delivery sequencing. The salesperson who manages the project earns the trust and the repeat business.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating luxury selling, ask:

Does the salesperson adapt their posture for luxury customers — or use the same approach as retail?
Do they understand the consultation timeline and multi-stakeholder dynamic?
Are they building relationships with designers and architects — or just waiting for walk-in traffic?
Do they manage luxury projects with the coordination and attention the tier demands?
